To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
U.S. investors have a strong preference for value stocks and a strong preference for foreign equity markets that are small, liquid, and have high expected growth.
U.S. investors have been underweight in the foreign equity markets and that their portfolios have outperformed a foreign equity benchmark by a significant margin.

(i) investors do not exhibit the returns-chasing behavior that is commonly assumed in the literature; and (ii), contrary to the literature, U.S. institutional investors' foreign equity portfolio weights are positively correlated with future performance, consistent with a rational, forward-looking behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the behavior and performance of U.S. investors in the foreign equity market.
the question of whether U.S. investors have been successful in their international equity investments.
the question of whether the returns of U.S. investors who invest in foreign equity markets differ from the returns on foreign equity markets themselves.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
U.S. investors are not irrational in their international equity investments.
U.S. investors have not chased returns, and have not been late to the party.

U.S. international equity investors have been net buyers of foreign equity markets, and that their foreign equity portfolios have performed well relative to the market-weighted foreign equity benchmark.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the U.S. equity investor's foreign portfolio is not a "buy the losers and sell the winners" portfolio, and that it is not the case that U.S. investors are "buying the world's losers and selling the world's winners" either.
U.S. investors have not chased past winners, and that their portfolios have performed relatively well.
U.S. investors have done well in their international equity investments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
U.S. investors have not been passive investors in foreign equity markets.
U.S. investors, despite their limited access to international equity markets, were able to generate superior performance by investing in a portfolio that was not value-weighted.
the U.S. investor is an important driver of international equity market returns.
